# Experimental durable actors v1

This is the first executable substrate for BeamScale's Erlang-backed
Durable-Object-style service. It remains a special execution class of the same
FaaS deployment and route system.

## Identity and placement

A logical object is identified by:

`{tenant_id, application_id, namespace, object_key}`

The identity is hashed deterministically into the route's virtual-shard count.
The virtual shard is then mapped to an actor bucket. The actor key includes the
tenant, so an actor can multiplex many virtual shards and objects but can never
mix tenants.

The current defaults come from the common experimental profile contract:

- 4096 virtual shards
- 64 shards per actor

## Actor lifecycle

`bmscl_durable_registry` lazily starts one trusted platform actor per actor key.
Starting an actor pins the exact FaaS deployment generation using the existing
`bmscl_deployment_manager`. That generation remains non-GC-able until the
actor exits or is evicted.

Each actor serializes turn admission through a `gen_server` call and emits a
turn token containing a fencing epoch plus monotonically increasing sequence.
This is the hook that a later state/handler adapter will use to enforce
single-threaded object turns.

## Experimental limits in this PR

This PR intentionally does not pretend the service is fully durable yet.

- actor epochs are monotonic only within the current runtime instance
- no Postgres/Cockroach state adapter or local WAL is wired yet
- no alarms, outbox, idempotency table, or WebSocket hibernation yet
- no hot-shard splitting or cross-node lease service yet
- the actor currently provides placement/lifecycle/turn admission, not tenant
  handler execution

Those pieces can be added behind this interface without changing the ordinary
BeamScale lambda path or the Phoenix connection profile.

# Experimental FaaS special cases

BeamScale keeps the ordinary short-lived BEAM function as the default execution
model. This document defines two opt-in profiles that reuse the same deployment,
route, generation, capability, and isolation machinery while changing lifecycle.

## Phoenix v1

`experimental_profile = phoenix_v1` supports two execution classes:

- `request`: normal BeamScale FaaS invocation. Phoenix HTTP routes that do not
  require a persistent connection stay on the existing one-shot path.
- `connection`: WebSocket/LiveView transport lifecycle. The gateway or Phoenix
  adapter registers the actual transport process with
  `bmscl_http_router:register_connection/4`. The process pins its exact
  deployment generation until it exits. New generations do not migrate live
  sockets; operators drain them explicitly with
  `bmscl_phoenix_connections:drain_deployment/2`.

This PR deliberately does not claim full Phoenix release discovery or Plug/Cowboy
integration yet. It establishes the lifecycle contract that those adapters use.

## Durable actor v1

`experimental_profile = durable_actor_v1` reserves the
`durable_actor` execution class. A route must declare a namespace and receives
a deterministic virtual-shard layout. The follow-up durable-runtime PR supplies
the tenant-only actor placement and routing implementation.

Defaults are 4096 virtual shards and 64 shards per actor so a single tenant actor
may multiplex many shards without ever mixing tenants.

## Opt-in gate

Both profiles are disabled by default. Runtime execution requires:

```erlang
application:set_env(
  bmscl_supervisor,
  experimental_faas_profiles,
  [phoenix_v1, durable_actor_v1]
).
```

Route manifests may be staged before the gate is enabled, but the runtime refuses
to enter an experimental execution path until its profile is explicitly enabled.

# MicroVM runtime contract v1

Phoenix and Durable Actor execution use the same BeamScale FaaS control plane,
but dispatch into a Firecracker worker/launcher instead of the dense shared
bare-process executor.

## Host-to-worker admission ticket

Before a Firecracker operation is dispatched, `bmscl_experimental_runtime`
normalizes the route, checks the experimental profile gate, verifies the
Firecracker execution class, and issues a short-lived signed contract.

The signed claims bind:

- backend (`firecracker`)
- operation (`invoke_async`, `register_connection`, or `locate_durable_actor`)
- tenant id
- deployment id when present
- experimental profile and execution class
- the exact runtime authority manifest
- single-tenant microVM isolation
- issued-at / expiry timestamps
- a cryptographic nonce

The ticket is HMAC-SHA256 signed with `microvm_contract_secret`. That secret
belongs to the trusted host control plane / Firecracker launcher and must never
be injected into the tenant guest.

## Worker-side verification

The trusted launcher calls `bmscl_execution_policy:admit_microvm/3` before
starting or reusing a VM. Admission fails unless:

- the target is Firecracker-class
- a signed microVM contract is present
- the signature is valid
- the operation matches
- the worker's tenant identity matches the ticket tenant
- the ticket is still within its short TTL

This prevents a Phoenix or Durable Actor route from being redirected into the
shared bare-process pool and prevents one tenant's ticket from being replayed
against another tenant's VM.

## Guest authority

After host-side verification, the launcher may inject the sanitized authority
claims into the guest bootstrap.

For `phoenix_v1`, that authority permits normal BEAM/OTP process creation but
keeps OS process spawning, native code, ambient host filesystem access, and
unscoped network access denied by default.

For `durable_actor_v1`, BEAM process creation is platform-managed so tenant code
cannot silently create background processes that violate serialized durable
turn semantics.

## Filesystem baseline

Firecracker guests should be provisioned with:

- immutable/read-only application release
- quota-limited writable temporary storage
- no host filesystem mounts
- persistent storage only through an explicit BeamScale capability/adapter
- minimal `/dev`, restricted `/proc`, and no privileged host-management socket

## Replay hardening

v1 uses short ticket lifetimes plus tenant/operation binding. A later worker
registry can additionally persist recently consumed nonces for strict one-time
admission when a dispatch path requires replay prevention beyond the TTL.

# Provider portability: AWS Lambda and GCP Cloud Run

BeamScale's provider runtime preserves the P1/P2/P3 execution model while
treating the cloud execution environment as replaceable infrastructure.

    provider execution environment
      BEAM VM
        P1 bmscl_sup (grandaddy)
          P2 bmscl_runtime_sup (daddy)
            verified provider bundle
            middleware generation
            route generation
            provider ingress
            P3 fresh invocation process per worker call

Native BeamScale remains the default. Provider mode is opt-in with
BMSCL_PROVIDER_MODE=aws-lambda, aws-lambda-managed, or gcp-cloud-run.

## Immutable provider bundle

Provider startup requires BMSCL_PROVIDER_BUNDLE to name a
bmscl.provider.bundle.v1 manifest. The bundle binds:

- every Lambda/middleware (kind,name,build_sha256);
- the canonical route-manifest semantics;
- ordered request middleware;
- a monotonically chosen bundle generation.

Startup rejects path traversal and symlinked bundle paths, re-verifies every
artifact through the normal bmscl_artifact admission path, requires the runtime
deployment id to equal the declared build digest, verifies the route file
digest, verifies the full bundle digest, installs middleware holds, and only
then activates routes and starts provider ingress.

The off-platform runtime has no BeamScale control plane available to issue a
BeamScale admission receipt. A customer-owned provider image must therefore
configure an explicit runtime trust root rather than silently weakening
verification. The intended profile is:

    {require_admission_receipt, false},
    {require_attestation, true},
    {trusted_signing_keys, [
        {<<"customer-build-key">>, <<"<64 lowercase hex public key>">>}
    ]},
    {require_trusted_build_provenance, true}.

Exact provenance settings remain deployment policy. An unsigned or
self-declaring artifact must not become trusted merely because it is inside an
OCI image.

## Middleware v1

P2 owns bmscl_middleware_chain. A generation is an ordered list of exact
deployment ids held against GC. Each HTTP request checks out exact pins before
execution, so a hot middleware replacement cannot split one request across
generations.

Middleware is request-gate middleware in v1:

- 204 with an empty body means continue unchanged;
- any other valid Hosted response short-circuits the request;
- a 204 with a non-empty body, malformed response, timeout, or worker error
  fails closed.

Middleware runs as separately admitted/metered P3 work. The route Lambda is
invoked only after the chain continues. This keeps tenant code out of P2 while
still letting P2 hot-swap the exact middleware generations it dispatches.

bmscl_http_router:invoke/5 is the public HTTP path and always applies
middleware. invoke_async/4 is deliberately documented as a trusted route-only
primitive and must not be exposed directly as public/provider ingress.

## AWS Lambda

bmscl_provider_runtime validates AWS_LAMBDA_RUNTIME_API and starts Runtime API
pollers only after bundle activation.

For ordinary Lambda the runtime uses one poller. For aws-lambda-managed,
BMSCL_AWS_RUNTIME_CONCURRENCY may select 1-64 pollers (default 8), allowing the
trusted BEAM VM to admit concurrent requests while each request still gets a
fresh P3.

The adapter accepts API Gateway HTTP API payload format v2, supports binary
bodies without transcoding, maps repeated Set-Cookie response fields to the v2
cookies array, honors the Lambda deadline, and never includes Erlang exception
terms or stack traces in provider-facing errors.

P1/P2 lifetime is bounded by the AWS execution environment. Correctness cannot
depend on reuse.

## GCP Cloud Run

Cloud Run mode starts a trusted Cowboy listener on 0.0.0.0:$PORT after bundle
activation. Request bodies are capped at 16 MiB and normalize through the same
Hosted ABI used by AWS/native ingress.

Cloud Run may deliver concurrent requests to one container; those requests
naturally fan into independent P3 processes. P1/P2 may remain warm for the
container lifetime but are not durable state.

The v1 Cloud Run response adapter fails closed when a response contains multiple
Set-Cookie fields because Cowboy's map response API cannot preserve that
representation without parsing cookie semantics. AWS v2 does preserve multiple
cookies. This difference is surfaced as a conformance limitation rather than
silently corrupting headers.

## Lifecycle

Provider transport is a conditional child at the end of P2. P1 remains the same
outer supervisor. A planned Daddy replacement drains invocation work before the
provider child is stopped and recreated; the replacement starts empty and must
re-activate its provider bundle before accepting traffic again.

No provider execution environment is application persistence. Durable state
continues to live behind explicit capabilities/services.

# Runtime profiles, versioned environment snapshots, and logging

This document fixes the control-plane/runtime contract for BeamScale's three
execution classes while keeping the stable `bmscl_sup` ("granddaddy") small.

## Runtime hierarchy

```text
BEAM OS process
└── bmscl_sup                         stable bootstrap / Granddaddy
    └── bmscl_runtime_sup             replaceable Daddy
        ├── deployment manager
        ├── environment snapshot cache
        ├── authority + capability services
        ├── route services
        ├── budget/telemetry services
        ├── Phoenix connection runtime
        ├── Durable actor runtime
        └── invocation supervisor
```

Granddaddy must not own Redis clients, tenant environment state, routes,
deployment state, log queues, Durable Object ownership, KMS integration, or
customer policy. Daddy is disposable and must be reconstructable from external
desired state.

Tracked by #69.

## Code + configuration identity

A runnable workload is never identified only by a deployment generation.
Admission pins:

```text
{deployment_generation, env_version}
```

Environment versions are immutable. The current version is a pointer, not a
mutable map. If version 42 is required and only version 41 is present, admission
must fail closed or fetch 42 through the trusted provider. It must never silently
start with 41.

The first runtime primitive is `bmscl_env_cache`. It deliberately has no Redis,
KMS, database, or secret-store authority. It stores exact resolved snapshots for
Daddy and rejects conflicting writes to an existing version. The external
provider/distribution path is tracked by supervisor #67 and infra #29.

Tenant configuration must not be written with `os:putenv/2` inside a shared
BEAM VM. Hosted code receives configuration through scoped context/capability
APIs; process-global OS environment belongs to the trusted runtime only.

## Logging boundary

Tenant code logs through BeamScale, not directly to CloudWatch or another vendor.

```text
tenant actor/logger/stdout
        |
        v
trusted bmscl log boundary
        |
        v
local host telemetry collector
        |
        +--> CloudWatch (platform/security initially)
        +--> durable archive
        +--> customer log backend
```

Trusted log attribution may include invocation/root/parent IDs, tenant/shard,
runtime epoch, deployment id, env version, execution class, actor/object/
connection identity, region/host identity and policy digest. Capability tokens,
secrets and plaintext environment bundles are never metadata.

`bmscl_host_log` owns the runtime-side safe metadata allowlist. Host exporter,
stdout/group-leader capture, backpressure and durable delivery are tracked by
supervisor #68 and infra #31.

## Execution classes

| class | lifecycle | tenant process model | default placement |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `faas` | request, <= platform timeout | one tenant BEAM process per invocation | high-density proc-isolated BEAM |
| `phoenix` | long-lived application/connections | normal tenant OTP tree inside one tenant guest | single-tenant Firecracker microVM |
| `durable` | long-lived/hibernatable object actors | platform-managed object actors/shards | Firecracker tenant/shard-group microVM |

Phoenix remains Firecracker-only and may create normal in-guest OTP processes
without receiving ambient OS-process or native-code authority. Durable Actors
are also Firecracker-only; tenant turn concurrency and BEAM process creation
remain platform-managed. Global durable ownership/fencing and host placement
remain separate implementation concerns.

## Daddy replacement

Daddy can be replaced whenever needed, including daily. There is no periodic
restart requirement. Planned replacement drains local work, installs trusted
runtime code, starts a fresh Daddy, reconciles externally retained desired state,
performs a health invocation and only then returns the shard to routing.

Zero-downtime runtime updates use a second warmed runtime/shard and traffic
handoff. Granddaddy does not run two competing Daddy trees.

## Language boundary

Execution class is independent of source language. The intended signed-profile
matrix is owned by `bmscl-compiler` #25/#26/#27. The current runtime must
continue to fail closed on profile/language combinations it does not understand.

# Stable bootstrap and replaceable runtime

## Responsibility and release boundaries

| Layer | Owner | Expected change cadence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Host service and tenant microVM | runtime host in `bmscl-infra` | host/kernel/VM maintenance |
| BEAM VM and OTP application | trusted guest launcher | OTP/VM/security updates |
| `bmscl_sup` (granddaddy) | one static inner-child specification, OTP restart budget | months when healthy |
| `bmscl_runtime_sup` (daddy) and runtime modules | artifacts, admission, generations, budgets, requests | replaceable whenever needed, including daily |
| Worker generation | signed compiler artifact | each changed worker deployment |

The cadence is a design target, not an uptime guarantee or a periodic restart
job. Ship urgent fixes when needed. `bmscl_sup` is intentionally about twenty
lines; add operational logic to the runtime or the external release controller.
The runtime controller API is ordinary code executed by the caller, not another
permanent process inside the outer supervisor.

These are **Erlang processes in the same BEAM OS process**. The outer PID can
survive inner replacement; it cannot survive an emulator crash, OOM kill, guest
shutdown, OTP restart, or host reboot. The runtime host/guest service manager is
responsible for that boundary. This change does not implement that host service
or the still-pending host-to-guest invocation bridge.

## Planned release sequence

1. The trusted control plane removes this shard from new routing and retains its
   desired signed artifact identities outside the runtime. Drain outstanding
   fan-out trees at the ingress when possible; once local drain begins, new
   affine requests also receive `runtime_draining`.
2. Call `bmscl_runtime:stop(DrainTimeoutMs)` from a process **outside** the inner
   subtree. The deployment manager serializes admission and rejects new pins,
   artifact activation, rollback activation, and GC while draining. Existing
   pins may attach/release; requests remain under their current watchdogs.
3. Wait for `ok`. All pending pins and monitored invocations must finish before
   the inner supervisor is stopped. A timeout cancels the drain and returns
   `{error, drain_timeout}` without killing requests. The timeout bounds the
   drain wait; ordinary OTP control calls and subtree shutdown have their own
   latency. Supervisor children use `shutdown => infinity` so OTP can finish
   recursive shutdown rather than orphaning descendants.
4. Install the reviewed, compatible **trusted runtime** release using the
   deployment system/OTP release process. This repository exposes no API for
   downloading or loading arbitrary runtime code. Keep the outer module and
   application running; stopping the entire OTP application also stops the outer
   supervisor. Runtime `start_link/0` is the stable bootstrap ABI.
5. Call `bmscl_runtime:start()`. It uses the current `bmscl_runtime_sup` code and
   starts a fresh deployment manager, budget manager, and invocation supervisor.
   `restart/1` is a convenience for stop/start with already-installed code; it
   does not install a release.
6. Reactivate the desired artifacts through normal signature and digest
   verification. Verify the active deployment identity and a health invocation
   before putting the shard back in routing. The replacement returns
   `no_active_deployment` before activation. A running supervisor alone is not
   application readiness.

This is an explicit drain/restart/reactivate path with a serving gap. Zero-downtime
runtime replacement needs a separately warmed shard, readiness checks, routing
handoff, and external desired-state reconciliation. Those are control-plane work;
adding another OTP supervisor alone does not implement them.

## Failure semantics

- Outer restart intensity is three automatic inner restarts in sixty seconds.
  Exhaustion terminates the outer supervisor and escalates to the OTP
  application/guest host policy. No unbounded restart loop is hidden here.
- Inner restart intensity is five in ten seconds. Its services are `one_for_all`
  because deployment references and watchdog registrations must not be lost
  while old invocations continue. An invocation failure itself remains local:
  temporary request workers are never restarted or replayed.
- Shutdown order is invocation supervisor, budget manager, deployment manager.
  After an inner supervisor crash, its replacement waits up to ten seconds for
  the old registered services to exit before starting the new tree.
  A replacement manager soft-purges orphaned reserved slot modules before it
  accepts artifacts. It refuses startup if old code is still referenced; it
  never forcibly purges code from a surviving invocation.
- Automatic crash recovery starts with an empty registry, just like planned
  replacement. External desired state must restore admitted artifacts. Requests
  interrupted by an unplanned failure return errors; retry decisions, especially
  for writes, belong to the caller/control plane.
- A second drain coordinator is rejected while a drain is owned. Cancelling or
  killing the owner before the drain is sealed reopens admission. Lifecycle
  calls address the original manager PID so late cleanup cannot reopen a new
  manager. After sealing, owner loss leaves admission closed: complete the
  trusted `supervisor:terminate_child(bmscl_sup, bmscl_runtime_sup)` stop, then
  start/reactivate as above. Do not resume routing into an uncertain release.
- A failed `start/0` leaves the outer process available with its stopped child
  specification. Correct/revert the trusted release, retry `start/0`, then verify
  artifacts/readiness. Whole-VM upgrades require a separate host-level rollout.

## Verification

EUnit checks the exact outer PID across planned replacement and inner failure,
admission closure, timeout rollback, pending-pin drain, abandoned coordinator
cleanup, termination of requests after any coupled-service failure, and repeated
replacement/reload without stale slot code. This validates lifecycle mechanics;
it is not a months-long soak test or an end-to-end production release test.

OTP reference: [supervisor behaviour](https://www.erlang.org/doc/apps/stdlib/supervisor.html).
